meta.title: Who really said "I do not seek. I find"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Picasso's most-quoted line appears in Formes, Feb 1930 - but Pierre Daix found the 1926 Russian text behind it to be a pirated rework, not a Picasso letter.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I do not seek. I find'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is printed in Formes, February 1930, translated from a Russian text published under Picasso's name in 1926 - which Pierre Daix identified as a pirated reworking of a 1923 interview.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter & sculptor, co-founder of Cubism
answer.sourceLine: The wording is in print under Picasso’s name in his lifetime — but the document behind it is contested. “Je ne cherche pas, je trouve” appears in “Lettre sur l’art par Picasso” in the Paris review Formes, no. 2 (February 1930), which the editors introduce as extracts from a text published under Picasso’s name in the Moscow magazine Ogoniok (no. 20, 16 May 1926) and translated from the Russian by C. Motchoulsky (BnF Gallica ↗). It falls short of verified for a reason deeper than the translation chain: Pierre Daix’s Dictionnaire Picasso (1995) judges that Russian publication, put out by Gueorgui Iakoulov, “une reprise piratée et émaillée d’inventions” — a pirated reworking laced with inventions — of the authentic interview Picasso gave Marius de Zayas in 1923. So this is an interview text of doubtful provenance, not a letter Picasso wrote. English Wikiquote ↗ files the English form in its Disputed section, and Hélène Parmelin, who knew Picasso well, hedged on whether he ever said it at all.
answer.confidenceText: Attributed — and weakly. The words are in print under Picasso’s name in 1930, but Picasso scholarship treats the text they come from as a pirated rework of a 1923 interview rather than something he wrote.

source.heading: The printed source

docMeta.dd: Ogoniok, Moscow, no. 20, 16 May 1926 — a text published under Picasso’s name, per the editors’ note in Formes

Contested. Pierre Daix, Dictionnaire Picasso (1995), pp. 329–330, 488, 914, calls the Ogoniok interview, published by Gueorgui Iakoulov, a pirated and invention-laced reworking of Picasso’s authentic 1923 interview with Marius de Zayas
Formes: revue internationale des arts plastiques, no. 2, February 1930 — French Wikiquote cites p. 3; Citations vérifiées ↗ gives pp. 2 and 5 of the same issue
Russian into French by C. Motchoulsky; the English “I do not seek. I find” has no named translator

source.excerpt: On me prend d’habitude pour un chercheur. Je ne cherche pas, je trouve.
trail: May 1923 — The authentic text. Picasso makes the same argument in English, in “Picasso Speaks” in The Arts, vol. 3 (New York), edited by Marius de Zayas: “In my opinion to search means nothing in painting. To find is the thing.” Not yet the famous four words, but the identical thought, cited by Wikiquote at pp. 315–329 ↗.

16 May 1926 — A text published under Picasso’s name appears in the Moscow illustrated magazine Ogoniok (no. 20), alongside a photograph of the painter with his son. The editors’ note above the French text in Formes ↗ presents it as extracts from a letter signed by Picasso — a description later scholarship rejects.

February 1930 — The Paris review Formes runs “Lettre sur l’art par Picasso,” translated from the Russian by C. Motchoulsky: “On me prend d’habitude pour un chercheur. Je ne cherche pas, je trouve.” This is the earliest printing of the exact wording this page could locate, in BnF’s scan of the issue ↗ — French Wikiquote places it on p. 3, Citations vérifiées on pp. 2 and 5.

1995 — Pierre Daix, in the Dictionnaire Picasso (pp. 329–330, 488, 914), identifies the Ogoniok piece as an interview published by Gueorgui Iakoulov and describes it as “une reprise piratée et émaillée d’inventions” of the 1923 de Zayas interview — a pirated rework, salted with invention. Citations vérifiées ↗ independently calls the Formes text “un montage fantaisiste réalisé à partir de précédentes déclarations.”

Since — The line becomes, in Hélène Parmelin’s words, “la phrase de Picasso le plus souvent citée” — while she herself doubted he had ever pronounced it. English Wikiquote lists “I do not seek, I find” in its Disputed section ↗, citing only Graham Sutherland’s 1936 essay in Signature.
source.excerptNote: As printed in Formes, no. 2 (February 1930), under the heading “Lettre sur l’art par Picasso.” Sources disagree on the page: French Wikiquote cites p. 3, Citations vérifiées pp. 2 and 5, and BnF Gallica blocks automated readers, so we could not settle it ourselves. Literally: “I am usually taken for a searcher. I do not seek, I find.” That English rendering is ours — no published English translation of this text is attached to the famous line. The same sentence closes the essay a few pages later, immediately above the credit “(Traduit du Russe par C. Motchoulsky.)”

source.useLine: Free to use in the United States — the 1930 Formes text is public domain there. Outside the US the term runs from the author’s death, and Picasso died in 1973, so treat the text as in copyright in France and the rest of the EU until 2044 and check your local term before commercial reuse.
source.rightsNote: Both publications behind this line predate 1931 and are in the public domain in the United States: the Russian text in Ogoniok (1926) and the French rendering in Formes (February 1930), translated by C. Motchoulsky. This is a US finding only — outside the US the term runs seventy years from the author’s death (Picasso died in 1973), so material published under his name stays in copyright in France and the EU until 2044. The bare four-word English rendering has no identified translator and is not traceable to any one copyrighted edition. Note also that modern books and scholarly editions that reprint the essay — such as Gallimard’s Propos sur l’art (1998) — carry their own copyright in those editions.

author.name: Pablo Picasso
author.heading: Who Picasso was
author.metaLine: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter & sculptor, co-founder of Cubism
author.bio: Pablo Ruiz Picasso (25 October 1881 – 8 April 1973) was a Spanish painter and sculptor who spent most of his adult life in France, and who pioneered Cubism alongside Georges Braque. He was also one of the most heavily interviewed artists who ever lived, and much of what circulates as his “philosophy” comes to us secondhand — through interviewers, friends’ memoirs, and translations. He disliked being described as a searcher or experimenter, and the documented text behind this quote is his sustained argument against that word.

cite.sourceCitation: “Lettre sur l’art par Picasso,” trans. from the Russian by C. Motchoulsky, Formes: revue internationale des arts plastiques, no. 2 (February 1930): 3 (Citations vérifiées gives pp. 2, 5). Presented by the editors as extracts from a letter signed by Picasso, reprinted from Ogoniok (Moscow), no. 20, 16 May 1926 — but Pierre Daix, Dictionnaire Picasso (1995), 329–330, 488, 914, identifies that publication as a pirated, invention-laced reworking of Picasso’s 1923 interview with Marius de Zayas. English Wikiquote lists the English form, “I do not seek, I find,” in its Disputed section.

copyAttribution: I do not seek. I find. — attributed to Pablo Picasso. Printed in French as “Je ne cherche pas, je trouve” in “Lettre sur l'art,” Formes no. 2 (February 1930), translated from the Russian by C. Motchoulsky, from a text published under Picasso's name in the Moscow magazine Ogoniok in 1926 — which Pierre Daix identified as a pirated rework of Picasso's authentic 1923 interview with Marius de Zayas. English Wikiquote lists the English wording as disputed.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: The thought is Picasso’s; the four words may not be. Everything wrapped around them — the language, the medium, the document, and above all the certainty — comes apart on inspection.

items.why: The Formes editors call their text extracts from a letter signed by Picasso. Pierre Daix, in the Dictionnaire Picasso (1995), pp. 329–330, 488, 914, says otherwise: the 1926 Ogoniok piece was an interview published by Gueorgui Iakoulov and is “une reprise piratée et émaillée d’inventions” of the interview Picasso really gave Marius de Zayas in 1923. Citations vérifiées ↗ reaches the same verdict independently, calling it “un montage fantaisiste.” Every citation of this page as a Picasso letter — ours included, until this revision — inherits that problem.

The Spanish form circulates as though it were Picasso’s own words, and it looks native because he was Spanish. But the documented printed text is French, translated from Russian. Even Wikiquote’s Disputed entry ↗ prints the Spanish version first, with no Spanish source behind it.

It is almost always staged as a spoken retort delivered to someone. What exists is a printed text of contested authorship. Hélène Parmelin, who knew Picasso well, hedged precisely on this point when discussing the phrase — “si vraiment il l’a prononcée” (if he really said it) — as quoted by French Wikiquote ↗.

Most collections give no citation whatsoever. Russian Wikiquote ↗ lists “Я не ищу. Я нахожу.” under its heading for quotes without sources — ironic, given that the trail leads back to a Russian magazine.

The line is often footnoted to the 1923 de Zayas interview. That interview is the authentic text — and it does not contain the famous four words. It has a related but longer sentence, “In my opinion to search means nothing in painting. To find is the thing,” at pp. 315–329 of The Arts, as Wikiquote’s sourced 1923 section ↗ shows. The compression into an epigram happens somewhere downstream of Picasso.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest printing of the exact wording we could locate is Formes, no. 2, February 1930 ↗ — in French, translated from a Russian magazine piece published under Picasso’s name in 1926 that Pierre Daix judged a pirated rework of Picasso’s real 1923 interview.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Picasso spent his career being called a chercheur — a searcher, a researcher, an experimenter forever hunting for the next thing. He hated the word, and this line is the rebuttal. He made the case at length rather than in four words, in the interview he gave Marius de Zayas in 1923: he could hardly understand the importance given to the word research in modern painting, and in his opinion to search means nothing in painting — to find is the thing. The 1930 French text carries the same argument, extended: that the spirit of research poisoned those who, failing to understand the positive side of modern painting, tried to paint the invisible, and that he tries to represent what he has found and not what he is looking for. Whether those extended words are his is the open question below.

What survived into circulation is the punchline with the argument stripped off, restaged as a spoken boast. Read in place, it is less arrogance than irritation — a painter refusing a label that made his finished work sound provisional.
context.detailsSummary: The broken chain, and why it matters
detailsBody: The route from Picasso to the English epigram runs through at least three languages and one document nobody can vouch for. A text published under Picasso’s name appeared in Russian in Ogoniok in Moscow in May 1926. In February 1930 the Paris review Formes printed extracts in French, translated from the Russian by C. Motchoulsky. The English “I do not seek. I find” is a later rendering of that French, with no translator’s name attached to it anywhere we could find.

The weak link is not the translating, it is the first step. Pierre Daix’s Dictionnaire Picasso (1995) treats the Ogoniok piece as an interview published by Gueorgui Iakoulov and calls it a pirated version of the 1923 de Zayas interview, laced with inventions; the French verification project Citations vérifiées reaches the same conclusion, calling it a fanciful montage assembled out of earlier statements. So the sharpest wording of Picasso’s most-quoted line may have been sharpened by someone who was not Picasso — and a four-word aphorism is exactly the shape that survives, and rewards, that kind of handling.

None of which makes the citation fringe: French Wikiquote cites the passage to Formes and to Picasso, Propos sur l’art, edited by Marie-Laure Bernadac and Androula Michael (Gallimard, 1998), the standard collected edition of Picasso’s own statements — while attaching Daix’s warning to it. The line has been quoted in English since at least Graham Sutherland’s 1936 essay in Signature, which is the single English source Wikiquote cites for it. A widely reprinted text and an authentic one are different things, and this is the gap between them.
context.pull: “J’essaie de représenter ce que j’ai trouvé et non ce que je cherche.”
